title: Russia and the US Veto Each Other's Resolutions and Let MINURSO's Mandate Lapse, as Moscow Stalls Talks in Atlanta and Qatar Drafts a Nuclear Deal for Tehran
subhead: The Security Council failed to renew the Western Sahara mission after an unprecedented double veto, the first time the MINURSO file has broken down outright. In Atlanta, Lavrov froze the G20, and in Tehran a Qatari-brokered framework has begun to take written shape.

sections.heading: Western Sahara: the Security Council vetoes itself into an unmonitored ceasefire
sections.body:
The Security Council failed on Friday 30 October to renew the mandate of MINURSO, the UN mission that has monitored the Western Sahara ceasefire since 1991. Russia vetoed a US-drafted resolution; the United States then voted against a rival Russian text that would have simply extended the mission for a year. Neither draft reached the nine votes needed. The mandate expires on 31 October.

The substance matters more than the procedure. According to the text of the US draft reviewed by Western Sahara Resource Watch, Washington proposed extending the mission to 31 October 2027 but also wanted to strip the word 'Referendum' from its name, requested options for cutting uniformed personnel and closing team sites, and made Morocco's autonomy proposal under Moroccan sovereignty the sole basis for continued negotiations. France backed it, with its ambassador stating that Western Sahara is already part of Morocco. Russia's counter-draft made no reference to autonomy and reaffirmed self-determination, citing the Secretary-General's envoy Staffan de Mistura.

This is the first time the two permanent members have tabled competing texts and vetoed each other on this file. Renewals had previously been negotiated through the Group of Friends of Western Sahara and adopted by consensus; Russia began abstaining in 2018 and China abstained in 2025. WSRW notes that a short technical rollover is one possible way out, but no compromise had been confirmed as of Saturday morning.
sections.whyItMatters: MINURSO is one of the last functioning constraints on a 50-year-old territorial dispute. If the mandate lapses, ceasefire monitoring and mine action in a 266,000 sq km contested territory lose their legal basis, and Polisario and Rabat lose the only third party that verified the line. It also establishes a precedent: a UN peacekeeping mission can now be killed not by the party on the ground but by great-power competition over what the mission is allowed to say.

sections.heading: Atlanta: Lavrov arrives, the family photo is cancelled, and the G20 admits it has no consensus
sections.body:
At the G20 foreign ministers' meeting in Atlanta, hosted by Secretary of State Marco Rubio, Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov's presence — at Rubio's own invitation — dominated the two-day session. British Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband addressed Lavrov directly, saying that Russian drones had killed 15 people the previous day and that 'we all know you are the aggressor.' German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul said a photograph with Lavrov was unacceptable because 'there is no normalcy with Russia.' US officials confirmed the traditional family photo was skipped after European ministers refused to be photographed with him; one Western diplomat told Reuters that a third of members objected, naming Australia and Canada.

Lavrov said Moscow's position on Ukraine was unchanged and that Russia could not accept Ukraine as a military threat to its security interests. The meeting is expected to end with a chair's statement rather than a joint declaration, with Western officials saying the effort is now focused on a leaders' declaration for the Miami summit on 14-16 December.

On substance, the war with Iran set the economic agenda: Reuters reported that two Western officials said members broadly agreed on the severity of the energy shock and feared that renewed US strikes on Iran would push oil sharply higher. On Saturday, ministers were due to take up critical minerals and supply chains, where Rubio has promoted the 'Pax Silica' initiative against Chinese dominance of rare earth processing. The Quad — the US, India, Japan and Australia — meets in Atlanta on Saturday on the G20's margins.
sections.whyItMatters: A G20 that cannot produce a joint communique on two simultaneous wars has stopped functioning as a crisis-management body. The workaround visible here — ad hoc coalitions signing statements outside the consensus process — is how the US is now trying to run economic statecraft, and it is a much weaker instrument than a communique.

sections.heading: Tehran: a Qatari delegation arrives with a Vance letter and a seven-day draft
sections.body:
A Qatari delegation led by a senior adviser to the prime minister and foreign minister arrived in Tehran on Friday morning, coordinating with Washington, according to Iran's state agency IRNA. The delegation reportedly carried a letter from Vice President JD Vance to Iranian security official Mohsen Rezaei, which was welcomed in Tehran as a fresh diplomatic pathway to avert further US strikes.

Also on Saturday, Al Arabiya English reported a preliminary US-Iran framework, obtained exclusively by the outlet, that would move Iran's stockpile of highly enriched uranium to a third country or blend it down, reopen the Strait of Hormuz to international shipping within seven days of an initial understanding, and shift direct talks from Istanbul to Doha. China is named as a potential guarantor. The draft pairs Iranian commitments on the nuclear programme and maritime security with US steps to ease sanctions, blockades and other economic restrictions, and includes staged independent verification plus a dispute-resolution mechanism involving mediators and guarantors. These terms are a reported draft; neither government has confirmed them.

Trump's public position pulled in the opposite direction. Speaking in the Oval Office, he said Washington was in no hurry — 'we've been there for seven months' — and claimed Iran could not pay its soldiers or police, while declining to give figures for his assertion that the campaign's cost had been more than recovered elsewhere. Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan met Rubio on the G20 sidelines in Atlanta to discuss the negotiations.
sections.whyItMatters: The draft is the first written structure to emerge in seven months of war, and its seven-day Hormuz trigger is the part that matters economically. But the gap between Vance's letter and Trump's public 'no hurry' line is the story: any deal will have to survive a US administration that is simultaneously signalling both a settlement and a further strike package.

sections.heading: Hormuz: four tankers burn, and the IRGC says they used 'unauthorised routes'
sections.body:
The IRGC said four oil tankers caught fire and exploded in the Strait of Hormuz while travelling along what it called unauthorised routes, Al Jazeera reported on Saturday. The claim follows Friday's rescue of 25 crew from a burning tanker by Omani authorities, and a week in which mines have already been the operating tool of closure.

Al Jazeera also reported that US senators were briefed on what it characterised as Trump's plan to restart the war on Iran. Trump said separately that the war 'is going to get wrapped up soon' and that Washington needs a guarantee there will never be a nuclear weapon — a demand that sits awkwardly with the staged, verified concessions described in the Qatari-tracked draft.
sections.whyItMatters: Traffic through Hormuz is now being policed by the party that closed it: the IRGC is defining which routes are legal and burning ships that use others. That is a de facto licensing regime over roughly a fifth of global oil trade, and it would survive a ceasefire unless the reopening terms in the draft are enforced by someone other than the IRGC.

sections.heading: Kherson: Oleshky empties under the war's longest ceasefire, and a Ukrainian ombudsman crosses into Russia
sections.body:
Hundreds of Oleshky residents were evacuated on Friday under a humanitarian ceasefire brokered by US First Lady Melania Trump that has now held across the entire Kherson frontline region since Tuesday — the longest and most widespread truce since Russia's 2022 invasion, per the BBC. A convoy of 25 buses gave residents a four-hour window to leave, with ambulances for those with limited mobility; Russian human rights ombudsman Yana Lantratova said the operation passed 'without any incidents' and that an estimated several hundred chose to stay.

The evacuation route is itself the story: evacuees travel through Russian-occupied territory to Anapa in southern Russia, fly to Gomel in Belarus, and cross by road into Ukraine's Chernihiv region. Ukraine's ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets travelled to Oleshky from Armiansk in occupied Crimea and, per the BBC, becomes the first Ukrainian official since the war began to visit Russian-occupied territory and then Russia itself. Lantratova and Lubinets jointly asked for such missions to become regular under Melania Trump's coordination.

Moscow moved quickly to bound the precedent. Peskov's office indicated on 30 October that the Oleshky arrangement offers no clear path to wider agreements, and Lavrov told the G20 the Russian position on Ukraine was unchanged.
sections.whyItMatters: This is the first functioning Russia-Ukraine channel of the war, and it runs through Washington rather than through European mediators. It also normalises direct Russian-Ukrainian official contact in occupied territory — a small, real shift in how the war might one day be unwound, and one the Kremlin is deliberately keeping small.

sections.heading: The rest of the board: Patriot interceptors for Kyiv, a defence bank charter, and Aden under missile fire
sections.body:
The State Department approved a $2.1bn sale of 500 Patriot PAC-3 MSE interceptors to Ukraine on Friday, funded by Canada, Germany, Norway and the EU loan rather than US money. The European Commission separately proposed a 45bn euro Ukraine Support Loan for 2027, with 31.7bn for Ukraine's defence industry and 13.3bn in budget support. Nine countries including Turkiye are set to sign a Canada-led multilateral defence bank charter in Luxembourg on 30 November, aiming to start lending in 2027.

In Yemen, Houthi missiles struck the vicinity of Al-Ma'ashiq Palace in Aden's Crater district on Friday, where the internationally recognised government is based, and air defences engaged drones over government institutions, a local security official told Xinhua. Government spokesman Majid al-Nuzaili said Aden International Airport was also targeted; the same compound took five missiles on 15 October, killing five. In the occupied West Bank, Israeli forces demolished two Palestinian homes in Hebron as an operation there entered its eighth day, with the Hebron governorate emergency committee reporting 537 families — 3,361 people — displaced from al-Jilda and Deir Baha.
sections.whyItMatters: The Patriot sale is the model that has replaced direct US aid to Kyiv: European and allied money, American hardware, no American appropriation. The Aden strikes show the Houthis now hold two capitals under fire at once while their missiles also reach Saudi infrastructure — a single militia sustaining two separate fronts.

bottomLine: The most consequential event of the day was procedural: the Security Council let MINURSO's mandate expire because Russia and the United States vetoed each other's versions of a routine renewal, killing the ceasefire monitor for Western Sahara and setting a precedent that great-power disagreement can now end a peacekeeping mission outright. Around it, the same pattern repeated in different registers: the G20 could not produce a joint communique because Europe would not be photographed with Lavrov; Iran and the US moved toward a written seven-day Hormuz framework in Doha and Qatar while the IRGC burned four tankers for using the wrong routes and Trump said he was in no hurry; and a US-brokered humanitarian truce in Kherson delivered a working Russia-Ukraine channel that Moscow immediately said leads nowhere else. The binding constraint this week is not the battlefield but the willingness of major powers to keep any shared instrument alive.
